nodes.title: Serverless functions: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Functions-as-a-Service (Lambda, Azure Functions, Cloud Functions) execute short-lived code in response to events. No servers, no patching, auto-scaling. The exam tests triggers, integration patterns, and the limits that bite at scale.

flashcards.front: Triggers — what fires a function?
flashcards.back: HTTP request (API Gateway, HTTP trigger), object storage event (file uploaded), queue message (SQS, Service Bus, Pub/Sub), schedule (cron / EventBridge), database stream (DynamoDB Streams, Change Feed). One function, many possible triggers — the runtime hands you the event payload.

flashcards.front: What is the function's execution context?
flashcards.back: The runtime environment that persists between invocations on the same warm instance. Things defined OUTSIDE the handler (DB connections, cached secrets, imported modules) are reused on the next invocation — huge perf win. Anything inside the handler runs every time.

flashcards.front: Idempotency — why does serverless need it?
flashcards.back: Most event sources retry on failure: SQS delivers at-least-once, S3 events can fire twice for a single upload, EventBridge retries on 5xx. Your function MUST tolerate the same event twice (use idempotency keys, conditional writes, dedup tables) or you'll double-charge a customer.

flashcards.front: Concurrency limits — what's the trap?
flashcards.back: AWS Lambda's account-level concurrency cap is 1000 by default. A sudden traffic spike can starve other functions in the account. Mitigations: reserved concurrency (guarantees a slice for a critical function), provisioned concurrency (pre-warmed instances), per-function quotas.

nodes.title: Command-line tooling: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Most exam workflows involve `aws`, `az`, `gcloud`, or `kubectl`. Knowing the structure of each (resource → command → flags) saves you in the lab portion and in real life. They're all roughly the same shape with different naming conventions.

flashcards.front: How do you authenticate the AWS CLI?
flashcards.back: `aws configure` writes credentials to `~/.aws/credentials` (access key + secret) and `~/.aws/config` (region, output format). Use named profiles for multi-account: `aws s3 ls --profile prod`. Prefer `aws configure sso` or temporary STS credentials over long-lived access keys.

flashcards.front: What does `kubectl get` do, and what flags are essential?
flashcards.back: Lists resources of a kind: `kubectl get pods`, `kubectl get nodes`. Key flags: `-n <namespace>` (default is `default`), `-o wide` (more columns), `-o yaml` (full manifest), `--watch` (live updates), `-l label=value` (filter by label).

flashcards.front: Output formatting — JSON, table, text?
flashcards.back: AWS / Azure / gcloud all support `--output json|text|table|yaml`. JSON is for piping into `jq` for scripts. Table is for humans browsing in the terminal. Always set a default in your config so you don't squint at JSON when browsing.

flashcards.front: How do you find a command's options without leaving the terminal?
flashcards.back: `aws <service> <command> help` (or `--help`), `kubectl <verb> --help`, `az <group> <command> --help`. These open built-in docs with every flag listed. Searching the official web docs is for concepts; for syntax, the local help is always current.

nodes.title: State: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on State. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: Terraform tracks the mapping between configuration resources and real-world infrastructure IDs in a STATE file (default `terraform.tfstate`). Without state, Terraform couldn't (a) know what's already created, (b) detect drift, (c) plan deletions. Best practice: store state REMOTELY (S3, Terraform Cloud) with locking + encryption. Which describes state?
flashcards.back: State: Terraform's source of truth. Contains: resource IDs (aws_instance.web → i-1234567890), dependencies, provider metadata, module structure. Remote state (S3+DynamoDB, Terraform Cloud) enables team collaboration and locking. Never manually edit state — use terraform state commands.

flashcards.front: Terraform automatically writes the PREVIOUS state to a sibling file before each state-mutating operation. If a state save is corrupted or accidentally rolled back, the previous version can be restored. The file name uses a `.backup` suffix. Which file?
flashcards.back: tfstate.backup: created before terraform apply modifies state. Contains state from before this apply. One-level safety net. For teams: use remote state with versioning (S3 with versioning enabled, Terraform Cloud). terraform state commands modify state — always backup first with: terraform state pull > backup.tfstate.

flashcards.front: A platform team has 5 engineers all running `terraform apply` against the same configuration. With LOCAL state, two simultaneous applies corrupt the state file. The fix: store state in a SHARED REMOTE BACKEND (S3 + DynamoDB lock, or Terraform Cloud, etc.) with encryption + access control. Which describes remote state + its value?
flashcards.back: Remote state backends: S3+DynamoDB (AWS), Azure Blob + Table, GCS, Terraform Cloud, Consul. DynamoDB: state locking (prevents concurrent applies). S3 versioning: state history. terraform_remote_state: read outputs from another state. Configure: terraform { backend 'S3' { bucket, key, region, dynamodb_table } }. Azure Storage, GCS, Terraform Cloud) instead of locally — enables: team collaboration (all members access same state), state locking (prevent concurrent applies), state versioning, access control, and cross-workspace state sharing via remote state data source

flashcards.front: Two engineers `terraform apply` simultaneously against the SAME remote state. Without protection their applies could race and corrupt state. The backend supports a LOCK — first apply acquires it (via DynamoDB lease, GCS atomic write, etc.), the second apply WAITS or fails. Lock released on apply completion. Which describes state locking?
flashcards.back: State locking: supported by most remote backends (S3+DynamoDB, Azure Blob, GCS, Terraform Cloud). Local backend: no locking. Lock timeout: -lock-timeout=10m. If lock not released (crash): force-unlock with ID from error message. Concurrent applies: second apply waits or fails depending on backend configuration. destroy, state operations), Terraform acquires a lock — prevents concurrent operations from corrupting state. With DynamoDB backend: creates lock entry. Lock released after operation completes. Force unlock: terraform force-unlock LOCK_ID (use with caution)

nodes.title: Providers: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on Providers. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: A `terraform` block declares `required_providers { aws = { source = "hashicorp/aws"; version = "~> 5.0" } }`. The version constraint uses operators: `=` exact, `!=` exclude, `>`, `>=`, `<`, `<=`, `~>` (pessimistic — major.minor pinned, patch free). Which describes Terraform provider version constraints?
flashcards.back: Version constraints: ~>3.0 (>=3.0, <4.0 — allow minor but not major). ~>3.2.0 (>=3.2.0, <3.3.0 — allow patch only). Best practice: pin major version (~>3.0), allow minor updates. Lock file: .terraform.lock.hcl records exact version used — commit to VCS for reproducibility. terraform init -upgrade: update to latest matching.

flashcards.front: Terraform writes a LOCKFILE `.terraform.lock.hcl` after `init`. It pins the EXACT version + SHA-256 checksums of every provider downloaded. Subsequent `init`s on other machines / CI verify the same versions + checksums — preventing silent provider upgrades + supply-chain swaps. Should be COMMITTED to version control. Which describes it?
flashcards.back: Lock file: introduced in Terraform 0.14. Records: provider version, constraints, checksums (sha256 hashes for all platforms). Commit to version control — ensures all team members and CI use identical provider versions. terraform init -upgrade: updates to latest matching versions, regenerates lock file. Never manually edit.

flashcards.front: A Terraform configuration needs to deploy AWS resources in TWO regions (us-east-1 + eu-west-1). Without intervention only ONE `aws` provider config can exist per module. Provider ALIASES let you declare multiple configurations of the same provider type. Resources select via `provider = aws.east`. Which describes aliases?
flashcards.back: Provider aliases: default provider (no alias), aliased providers (explicit alias). Resources use aliased provider: resource 'aws_instance' 'replica' { provider = aws.us-west }. Use cases: multi-region deployments, different accounts (dev/prod), different organizations. Modules inherit provider from root unless configured with providers argument.

flashcards.front: A team using Terraform across Linux + macOS + Windows wants the lockfile (`.terraform.lock.hcl`) to record checksums for ALL THREE OS platforms — so CI/CD on Linux + dev on Mac + ops on Windows verify against the same lock. `terraform providers lock -platform=linux_amd64 -platform=darwin_arm64 -platform=windows_amd64` adds those platforms' checksums. Which describes the command?
flashcards.back: terraform providers lock: update lock file with checksums for specified platforms. Use when: team uses Mac (arm64) + CI uses Linux (amd64) — run providers lock for both platforms so lock file works everywhere. Also: providers mirror (cache providers), providers schema (show schema), providers list (show configured providers).

nodes.title: Modules: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on Modules. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: A team has 5 VPCs with identical 'web-tier + app-tier + DB-tier' patterns. Copying the resource blocks across 5 directories is unmaintainable. They package the pattern as a REUSABLE GROUP of resources with INPUT variables (VPC name, CIDR) and OUTPUTS (subnet IDs), versioned in a registry. Other configs call `module "web_tier" { source = … version = … }`. Which Terraform concept?
flashcards.back: Modules: package reusable configurations. Call module: module 'vpc' { source='terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws', version='3.0' }. Inputs: module variables. Outputs: module outputs accessible in root as module.vpc.vpc_id. Local modules: relative paths. Benefits: DRY principle, tested patterns, team standardization.

flashcards.front: Best practices for Terraform module inputs / outputs: (a) TYPE every variable, (b) ADD descriptions + validation, (c) Use sensitive for secrets, (d) Default to least-permissive, (e) Output ONLY values consumers need, (f) Document with README + examples, (g) Pin module versions via Registry. Which describes the practices?
flashcards.back: Best practices: (1) Type all variables (string, number, bool, list, map, object). (2) Provide descriptions (visible in terraform-docs). (3) Set defaults for optional variables. (4) Validate expected values. (5) Outputs: expose IDs and ARNs callers need. (6) README: usage examples. (7) versions.tf: required_providers and required_version. (8) CHANGELOG for updates. provide descriptions, validate inputs, use sensible defaults. Module outputs: expose only what callers need (not everything), use sensitive attribute for secrets. Module structure: variables.tf, main.tf, outputs.tf, versions.tf, README.md

flashcards.front: The Terraform Registry hosts modules under a 3-part name + provider format: `module "vpc" { source = "terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws" }`. The format is `<NAMESPACE>/<MODULE>/<PROVIDER>`. Which describes the registry source format?
flashcards.back: Module sources: (1) Registry: 'terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws' with optional version. (2) GitHub: 'github.com/org/repo' or 'git::https://...'. (3) S3: 's3::https://bucket/module.zip'. (4) Local: './modules/vpc'. (5) Terraform Cloud private registry: 'app.terraform.io/ORG/vpc/aws'. Version pinning: always use version for registry modules in production. example: terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws (namespace=terraform-aws-modules, module name=vpc, provider=aws). Version: version='~>3.0'. Download: terraform init downloads from registry automatically

flashcards.front: A reusable module declares it ACCEPTS multiple provider configurations of the same type (e.g., a multi-region module taking `aws.east` + `aws.west`). The module's `terraform { required_providers { aws = { source = "hashicorp/aws"; configuration_aliases = [aws.east, aws.west] } } }` declares this. The root module then PASSES the provider configurations via `providers = { aws.east = aws.east, aws.west = aws.west }`. Which describes configuration_aliases?
flashcards.back: configuration_aliases: module defines required_providers { aws = { source='hashicorp/aws', configuration_aliases=[aws.us-east, aws.eu-west] } }. Root module: module 'multi_region' { providers = { aws.us-east = aws.us-east, aws.eu-west = aws.eu-west } }. Module resources use provider = aws.us-east. Enables clean multi-region module design.

nodes.title: Terraform Cloud: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on Terraform Cloud. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: HashiCorp Terraform Cloud is a managed SaaS that provides BEYOND open-source Terraform: (1) shared remote state with locking, (2) remote plan + apply execution (so secrets stay in the platform), (3) policy as code (Sentinel / OPA), (4) cost estimation, (5) VCS integration (auto-plan on PR, apply on merge), (6) team-based RBAC + audit, (7) private module registry. Which describes Terraform Cloud?
flashcards.back: Terraform Cloud (free tier available): remote state, remote execution (runs in HashiCorp infrastructure), VCS integration (GitHub/GitLab), cost estimation, private module registry. Teams: per-workspace access control, review and approval workflows. Terraform Enterprise: self-hosted version for air-gapped environments or compliance requirements.

flashcards.front: A team uses Terraform Cloud's `remote` backend. They run `terraform apply` from their laptop. Instead of running plan + apply LOCALLY, the CLI uploads the configuration to Terraform Cloud, which executes plan + apply in its own SECURE EXECUTION ENVIRONMENT (with provider credentials stored centrally), streams output back. Which describes the run workflow?
flashcards.back: Terraform Cloud runs: (1) CLI-driven: local terraform apply → run in TC → output streamed back. (2) VCS-driven: push to connected repo → automatic plan → manual/auto apply. (3) API-driven: trigger via API. Run queue: sequential per workspace. Logs: stored in TC for 6 months. Notifications: Slack, PagerDuty, email on state changes.

flashcards.front: HashiCorp ships THREE tiers of Terraform. (OSS) Free CLI, local plan / apply, no shared state or governance. (Cloud) Managed SaaS — remote state, remote runs, free tier + paid teams + governance. (Enterprise) On-prem deployment — same features as Cloud + private installation. Which describes the distinction?
flashcards.back: OSS: no cost, local terraform CLI, state in remote backend, team workflow via VCS. Terraform Cloud Free: 500 resource hours/month, 1 user, remote execution, state storage. Plus/Business: Sentinel, SSO, audit logs, more resources. Enterprise: self-hosted (runs in your data center), FIPS compliance, air-gapped, dedicated support, clustering for HA. basic collaboration via git+remote state. Cloud: free tier + paid tiers, remote execution, VCS integration, team access, Sentinel policies (paid), cost estimation, private registry. Enterprise: self-hosted Terraform Cloud, air-gapped, SAML SSO, audit logging, clustering, additional compliance features

flashcards.front: Terraform Cloud (TFC) supports VCS-DRIVEN workflows. Connect a TFC workspace to a GitHub / GitLab / Bitbucket repo. Pull requests trigger SPECULATIVE PLANS — TFC runs plan, posts the diff as PR comment. Merges to `main` trigger an APPLY automatically (with optional manual gate). Drift detection runs periodically. Which describes it?
flashcards.back: VCS workflow: PR → Terraform Cloud runs speculative plan → plan output shown in PR checks → review changes → merge → Terraform Cloud runs apply automatically. Plan includes: additions, changes, destructions. Team can review infrastructure changes like code changes. Integrates with branch protection rules.

nodes.title: Security fundamentals: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Security is about layering defenses so no single failure compromises a system. Most exams test the same core ideas: least privilege, defense in depth, the CIA triad, and the shared-responsibility line between you and your cloud provider.

flashcards.front: What is the CIA triad?
flashcards.back: Confidentiality (only the right people see the data), Integrity (data isn't tampered with), Availability (the system is reachable when needed). Every security control maps to at least one of these three pillars.

flashcards.front: What does 'least privilege' mean?
flashcards.back: Grant each identity (user, role, service account) the minimum permissions needed to do its job — no more. The opposite is wildcard access, which makes a single credential leak catastrophic.

flashcards.front: What is defense in depth?
flashcards.back: Stack multiple, independent controls so an attacker has to defeat all of them. Example: WAF in front of an app, network ACL on the subnet, IAM on the workload, encryption at rest in the database.

flashcards.front: Shared responsibility model — who does what?
flashcards.back: The cloud provider secures the cloud (physical hardware, hypervisor, region facilities). You secure what's IN the cloud (your data, IAM config, OS patching on EC2, application code). The exact line shifts by service: serverless is more on the provider, IaaS is more on you.
